total.amount: €1.5 million in July 2022, after €300,000 in November 2018

status.text: The checkout still quotes 97.80 euro, so the service is on sale. No news found in the last 12 months.

traction.text: Chantal van der Velde and Graciëlla van Vliet founded Closure in 2018. Before that, van Vliet worked as a part-time management trainee in China while pursuing a master's in econometrics and machine learning. The July 2022 funding note also spells her surname van Hamersveld. Closure raised 300,000 euro in November 2018 and 1.5 million euro in July 2022 from Borski Fund and Rabobank. It said it worked with more than 200 funeral homes. In January 2023 van Vliet said one in four Dutch deaths was reported through Closure.

who_pays.text: A family on Closure's own checkout pays 97.80 euro. Silicon Canals wrote in January 2023 that the service was free of charge to heirs because companies pay to offer it. Both descriptions are published, and they are not the same model. Funeral directors also refer families.

what_it_does.text: Closure collects one set of details after a death and asks companies to end or transfer the person's contracts, from phone and energy to insurers, charities, and social accounts. The family picks the organisations and tracks each request. A 2022 note says a Dutch financial-markets licence lets it notify banks and insurers.

why_interesting.text: Funeral directors and large service companies already speak to the family about one contract, and Closure uses that contact to offer the rest. The one-in-four figure is hers, from 2023, and the checkout price now charged to families was not the model in that interview.

competitors.difference: Unlike BYOND, where a person stores accounts for family to open after a death, Closure contacts the companies and asks them to end or transfer the contracts.

who_pays: The household pays. The site says documents, trusted contacts and one connected bank stay free, including if you stop paying, and that you pay for the gap-checking and for extra banks. Apple lists Eterny Premium at 199 Czech koruna a month or 1,990 Czech koruna a year.

what_it_does.text: Eterny keeps a household's bank accounts, insurance, home, crypto and papers in one private place, and warns about renewals, a blank beneficiary or cover that no longer matches the home. You choose who can open it, and when. The terms, from Eterny Legacy s.r.o. in Bystřice pod Hostýnem, describe it as a place for assets, wills and the people allowed to receive them. The site says files are encrypted on the phone before they are uploaded.

who_pays.text: The household pays. The site says documents, trusted contacts and one connected bank stay free, including if you stop paying, and that you pay for the gap-checking and for extra banks. Apple lists Eterny Premium at 199 Czech koruna a month or 1,990 Czech koruna a year.

traction.text: The about page says 17,000 households in the EU and the US use Eterny, and that the checking has looked at more than 100,000 assets. Apple shows 4.6 out of 5 from 9 ratings. A review dated 29 January 2026 called the app early, and the developer replied on 5 February 2026 that it was still in beta.

why_interesting.text: The free record and the family's access stay open if you cancel. You lose the warnings, not the papers. That is a different bet from a storage app that locks heirs out when the subscription ends. The 17,000 household figure is the company's own, next to nine public app ratings.

status.text: As of 5 October 2026 Eterny is on the Apple App Store, with version 2.15.0 listed on 25 September, after a 31 December 2025 build. The terms took effect on 1 December 2025.

status.text: The site takes requests on weekdays from 08:00 to 16:00 and names Jonas Behrend and Jamie Hartmann as managers. The January 2022 report said Inqbaker would keep the name. No news found in the last 12 months.

traction.text: Antonia Albert and her brother Nikolaus Albert founded Careship in Berlin in 2015 after their grandmother needed help. She studied business administration in the Netherlands and Switzerland and worked at Rocket Internet. The site says more than 150,000 visits and a Google rating of 4.4 out of 5. Care Inside reported on 31 January 2022 that they had raised 13 million euro, filed for insolvency in December 2021, and that Inqbaker would continue the firm from 1 February 2022 with more than 1,600 helpers.

who_pays.text: Families request the visits. Care insurance can be billed under sections 36, 39, and 45b of SGB XI, and a health insurer can pay household help under sections 38 and 24h of SGB V. Private customers file the invoice themselves. No public price. The sale is a direct request, and insurance or private pay can apply.

what_it_does.text: Careship finds a local helper for housework, company, and daily tasks. A person calls or sends a request, agrees the tasks, and starts without a long contract. The site says the same helper returns. Care Companion GmbH places self-employed helpers, and Careship Ambulant GmbH uses employed ones.

why_interesting.text: The insurer can be the payer, and the offer is one returning helper. The 2026 site still takes requests and names Jonas Behrend and Jamie Hartmann as managers rather than the founding siblings.

The clinic device is not sold as a wheelchair replacement.

research_summary: an online platform connecting neighbors for home assistance services in a flexible and easy way.
job: Helpper connects people in Flanders and Brussels who need a hand at home with neighbours who have been screened. The tasks are ordinary, not medical: cooking, shopping, small jobs, a lift to an appointment, company, or keeping an eye on someone. Older people use it to stay in their own home, and a family can also pay a relative who already helps. Helpers are at least 16, and the visits are insured with AG Insurance.
who_pays: The person asking for help pays the helper's hourly rate. On the page for older people, a 3-month membership is €14.99 a month and a 12-month membership is €9.99 a month, with no service fee. Without a membership that page adds a 20% service fee, plus 21% VAT on the fee. People with a Flemish disability budget (PVB or PAB) can set the hourly rate up to €50 and pay a 12% service fee plus 21% VAT. A worked example is 10 hours at €15, which comes to €171.78.

what_it_does.text: Helpper connects people in Flanders and Brussels who need a hand at home with neighbours who have been screened. The tasks are ordinary, not medical: cooking, shopping, small jobs, a lift to an appointment, company, or keeping an eye on someone. Older people use it to stay in their own home, and a family can also pay a relative who already helps. Helpers are at least 16, and the visits are insured with AG Insurance.

who_pays.text: The person asking for help pays the helper's hourly rate. On the page for older people, a 3-month membership is €14.99 a month and a 12-month membership is €9.99 a month, with no service fee. Without a membership that page adds a 20% service fee, plus 21% VAT on the fee. People with a Flemish disability budget (PVB or PAB) can set the hourly rate up to €50 and pay a 12% service fee plus 21% VAT. A worked example is 10 hours at €15, which comes to €171.78.

traction.text: Helpper says it has more than 7,000 screened helpers in Flanders and Brussels. Belgian filings for 2025 show 14.6 full-time staff, a gross margin of €2,603,104 and a profit of €1,408,987. Those accounts were filed on 17 June 2026, and the registry lists the company as active.

why_interesting.text: A family can pay a neighbour, or a relative they already know, for ordinary help, and people with a Flemish disability budget can use that budget for the same thing. The Belgian state recognises Helpper for its sharing-economy tax rules, so the pay is declared rather than handed over in cash. The helper can earn up to €7,890 gross this way in 2026 before a higher tax rate applies.
